title: Milestone 3 in R!
text:
A little intro
For Milestone 3, I have decided to perform some analysis on the Palmer Penguin dataset by Allison Horst:
Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.



Palmer Penguins Logo: allisonhorst.github.io




Exploring the penguins!
First, I am going to apply the relevant libraries that we are going to be using in this analysis.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

Next, let’s get a glimpse of what the penguins dataset looks like.

penguins

# A tibble: 344 × 8
   species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
   <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
 1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
 2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
 3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
 4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA
 5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
 6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
 7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
 8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6               195        4675
 9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1               193        3475
10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2               190        4250
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


The first thing I would like to do is find the average bill depths of each specie.

arrange_penguins<- penguins|>
            drop_na(species, bill_depth_mm)|>
            group_by(species)|>
            summarise(mean_bill_depth = mean(bill_depth_mm))|>
            arrange(mean_bill_depth)

arrange_penguins

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_bill_depth
  <fct>               <dbl>
1 Gentoo               15.0
2 Adelie               18.3
3 Chinstrap            18.4


Now, I’m going to plot it as a bar chart!

arrange_plot <- ggplot(arrange_penguins, aes(x = species, y = mean_bill_depth)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Bill Depths by Specie" )
arrange_plot








I do not like the order of this plot. I would like it to be in an ascending order. Let’s reorder the factors…

relevel_penguins <- arrange_penguins |>
                mutate(species = fct_relevel(species, "Gentoo", "Adelie", "Chinstrap"))

… and replot

relevel_plot <- ggplot(relevel_penguins, aes(x = species, y = mean_bill_depth)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Bar Chart after fct_relevel() function" )
relevel_plot








That’s better!


References
Horst AM, Hill AP, Gorman KB (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data. R package version 0.1.0. https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.3960218.

Why Data Science
My interest in Data Science was sparked during my undergraduate studies, where I first discovered how powerful data-driven decision-making can be. The field naturally brought together the exact skills, analytical thinking, and areas of knowledge I was eager to explore. Choosing to pursue it further was a seamless blend of my background and core professional curiosity.

text:
Outside of Data Science
When I’m not diving into data, you’ll usually find me baking up something delicious, picking up my guitar, or lost in a great book. I also love a good game, whether on a screen or a board. These creative outlets keep me balanced, inspired, and always curious.
